Chartres
SHAR-truh
n. (the French cathedral city whose twelfth-century school taught a generation, and whose glass survives nearly entire)
From the Gaulish tribe the Carnutes, through Latin Carnotum; the French form drops the final consonants in speech.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Chartres, south-west of Paris, was from the early eleventh century one of the leading cathedral schools of Europe. Bernard of Chartres, Thierry of Chartres and William of Conches taught there, and John of Salisbury, afterwards bishop of Chartres, left in his Metalogicon the best surviving account of how such a school worked — the grammar, the set authors, the slow reading. The cathedral itself burned in 1194, all but the west front and the crypt, which held the Sancta Camisa, a garment venerated as the Virgin's; the rebuilding was financed partly by pilgrims to that relic and completed with extraordinary speed, and it retains more of its original thirteenth-century glass than any other great church in France. The dictionary records Chartres for the school and the glass. The school was a genuine good, and the dictionary says so: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is a command, and “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8) licenses the attention these men gave to grammar and the poets. The relic that paid for the windows is another matter, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) settles it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; grammar as the art of speaking correctly; glass as a hard brittle transparent substance; a cloister school is given under school; and a garment as an article of clothing.

expand to see more

SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.

GRAMMAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.

GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies.

DIALECTIC, a. Logical; argumental; pertaining to the art of reasoning.

GARMENT, n. Any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, &c.

Phi 4:8 — "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things."

Eph 2:9 — "Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Modern Corruption

French cathedral city with a leading twelfth-century school and the most complete surviving medieval glass in France, rebuilt after the fire of 1194.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that careful learning is commanded, not merely tolerated. Paul tells Timothy to “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), and Philippians licenses the whole range of honest attention, “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8). The school of Chartres, teaching boys to read Virgil slowly, was doing something a Reformed conscience can approve.

The live temptation is to let the beauty of the result cover the means. The windows were paid for in part by pilgrims coming to a venerated garment, and that transaction is excluded by “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9). Chartres is therefore two things at once, and the rule for sorting them is “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the measure the school itself professed to serve.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek spoudazo (G4704), to be diligent; Greek semnos (G4586), honest, venerable; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Greek theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed.

expand to see more

Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to be diligent, to give diligence; “Study to shew thyself approved unto God”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Greek semnos (G4586) — honest, grave, venerable; “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just”, Philippians 4:8.

Greek hagnos (G0053) — pure, chaste; “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just”, Philippians 4:8.

Greek ergon (G2041) — a work, a deed; “Not of works, lest any man should boast.”, Ephesians 2:9.

Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; “All scripture is given by inspiration of God”, 2 Timothy 3:16.

Usage

"“whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Phi 4:8) — the licence for grammar and the poets."

"“Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) — what the relic transaction falls to."
